hero.title: Grammar you work out, not just memorise
hero.lead: Short units for IELTS and university students. Test yourself, notice the pattern in a real text, work out the rule, practise, then see how much you’ve improved. No sign-in.

A2.name: Elementary
A2.cando: Everyday topics: describing, comparing and talking about amounts.
A2.about: You can talk about familiar topics in simple sentences.

B1.name: Intermediate
B1.about: You can describe experiences and processes and give simple reasons and opinions.

B2.name: Upper-intermediate
B2.cando: Connecting ideas clearly for study and work.
B2.about: You can write clear, connected texts and explain a viewpoint. A typical level for starting university.

C1.name: Advanced
C1.cando: Concise, formal and emphatic academic writing.
C1.about: You can write well-structured, detailed academic texts and use language flexibly.

A2: Past simple: regular and irregular verbs
B1: Modal verbs: must, have to, should
B2: Modals of deduction: must have, might have
C1: Cleft sentences: What we found was…

related.d: Find and fix errors in real student writing
Short practice for a more academic style

pre.q: I have lived here ___ 2021.
She studied in Japan ___ two years.
My phone rang ___ the lecture.

notice.title: A student’s message
notice.instr: Tap every time word: for, since or during.
notice.text: I have studied English [[for]] six years, and I have lived in Perth [[since]] March. [[During]] my first month, I felt homesick. I have not visited my family [[since]] then, but we talk [[for]] an hour every Sunday.
notice.after: Look at what comes after each word: a length of time, a starting point, or an event?

discover.ctx: for six years · for an hour
discover.q: What comes after for?
discover.hint: Six years, an hour: how long?
discover.insight: for + a length of time: for six years, for an hour, for a long time.

discover.ctx: since March · since then · During my first month
discover.q: What comes after since, and what comes after during?
o: since + a starting point; during + an event or period (when it happened)
since + a length of time; during + a starting point
discover.hint: March is a point in time.
discover.insight: since + a starting point (since 2021, since Monday), usually with the present perfect. during + a noun for an event or period: during the lecture, during the summer.

rule.title: For, since, during
points: for + length of time: for three weeks, for ages.
since + starting point: since 2020, since I arrived (usually with have/has + past participle).
during + event or period, to say when: during the exam, during my first year.
ex: I have worked here for two years, since 2024. I learned a lot during my first month.
rule.watch: Don’t use during for how long: during three hours → for three hours.

practice.q: The library has been closed ___ Monday.
Please don’t talk ___ the exam.

practice.s: We waited {during} two hours for the bus.

practice.q: I haven’t seen him ___ last semester.
practice.why: Last semester = a starting point → since.
practice.hint: Is it a length of time or a starting point?

post.q: They have been married ___ ten years.
I fell asleep ___ the film.
He has worked here ___ he finished university.

produce.task: Write 2–3 sentences about your studies or your life now. Use for, since and during once each.
checklist: I used for with a length of time.
I used since with a starting point.
I used during with an event or period.
produce.model: I have studied at this university since February. I have lived with my cousin for three months. During my first week, I got lost on campus every day.

units.title: Fewer or less? Number or amount?
units.cando: Talk about quantities correctly in academic writing.

pre.q: There are ___ students in the class this year.
We have ___ time than we thought.
The ___ of cars in the city has increased.

notice.title: From a report on transport
notice.instr: Tap the words that talk about quantity.
notice.text: The [[number]] of people who drive to work has fallen. [[Fewer]] cars are on the roads, so there is [[less]] traffic in the morning. The [[amount]] of money spent on fuel has also dropped, and [[fewer]] accidents have been reported.
notice.after: Look at the nouns after each word: can you count them?

discover.ctx: fewer cars · fewer accidents · less traffic
discover.q: Which nouns go with fewer?
discover.hint: Can you count cars?
discover.insight: fewer + plural countable nouns; less + uncountable nouns.

discover.ctx: the number of people · the amount of money
discover.q: Which word goes with countable nouns?
discover.hint: People can be counted.
discover.insight: the number of + plural countable noun; the amount of + uncountable noun.

rule.title: Fewer, less, number, amount
points: Countable: fewer students, the number of students.
Uncountable: less time, the amount of time.
The number of + plural noun takes a singular verb: The number of students has increased.
rule.watch: <s>less students</s> → fewer students; <s>the amount of people</s> → the number of people.

practice.q: ___ people use cash these days.

practice.s: The {amount} of students who passed has increased.
practice.why: Students are countable → the number of.

practice.q: Electric cars produce ___ pollution.
The number of complaints ___ fallen.
practice.why: The number of + plural noun → singular verb.

post.q: This method uses ___ energy.
There were ___ mistakes in her second essay.
The ___ of rain this year was low.

produce.task: Compare your city now with ten years ago in 2–3 sentences. Use fewer, less, the number of and the amount of.
produce.target: fewer/less and the number of/the amount of
checklist: fewer / the number of + plural countable nouns.
less / the amount of + uncountable nouns.
The number of … has a singular verb.
produce.model: The number of cafés in my city has doubled, but there is less green space. Fewer people drive to the centre, and the amount of traffic has fallen.

units.title: Its or it’s?
units.cando: Avoid one of the most common writing errors.

pre.q: The company changed ___ name.
___ important to check your sources.
The study has ___ limitations.

notice.title: From a book review
notice.text: [[It’s]] a useful book for first-year students. [[Its]] main strength is [[its]] clear examples. However, [[it’s]] quite long, and [[its]] last chapter feels rushed.
notice.after: One form has an apostrophe and one doesn’t. What’s the difference?

discover.ctx: It’s a useful book. · it’s quite long
discover.q: What does it’s mean?
discover.hint: Try replacing it with “it is”.
discover.insight: it’s = it is / it has. The apostrophe shows a missing letter.

discover.ctx: Its main strength · its last chapter
discover.q: What does its show?
o: belonging to it (like his or her)
discover.hint: Its main strength = the book’s main strength.
discover.insight: its = belonging to it, like his and her. No apostrophe.

rule.title: Its or it’s?
points: it’s = it is / it has: It’s clear. It’s been a long day.
its = belonging to it: The city and its people.
Test: if you can say “it is” or “it has”, write it’s.
rule.watch: In formal academic writing, avoid contractions: write it is, not it’s. But its (possessive) is always fine.

practice.q: ___ been a difficult year.
Every plant needs ___ own space.

practice.s: {Its} clear that more research is needed.
practice.why: It is clear → it’s, or better, “It is” in formal writing.

post.q: The government defended ___ decision.
I think ___ going to rain.
post.why: It is going to rain → it’s.

post.q: The theory has ___ critics.

produce.task: Write 2–3 sentences about a city, a company or an app. Use its at least twice and it is once.
checklist: its (no apostrophe) = belonging to it.
it’s only means it is / it has.
In formal writing I wrote it is in full.
produce.model: Melbourne is famous for its coffee and its laneways. It is also known for its changeable weather.

units.title: Comparatives and superlatives
units.cando: Compare two things, or one thing with a whole group.

pre.q: Melbourne is ___ than Adelaide.
This is the ___ book I have ever read.
The library is ___ (quiet) than the café.

pre.s: This exam was {difficulter} than the last one.

pre.q: My essay is ___ than yours.

notice.title: Where is the best place to study?
notice.instr: Read the text. Tap every word or phrase that compares things.
notice.text: The new city library is [[bigger]] than the old one, and the seats are [[more comfortable]]. The campus café is [[cheaper]], but it is [[noisier]] than the library. For me, the [[best]] place to study is the room on the third floor. It is the [[quietest]] room in the building and it has the [[most comfortable]] chairs.
notice.after: Some words end in -er or -est, and some use more or most. Why? You’ll work it out next.

discover.ctx: bigger · cheaper · noisier · quieter
discover.q: These are short adjectives (big, cheap, noisy, quiet). How do we compare two things with them?
discover.hint: Look at the endings.
discover.insight: Short adjectives (one syllable, or two syllables ending in -y): add -er + than. noisy → noisier (y → i); big → bigger (double the last letter).

discover.ctx: more comfortable · the most comfortable
discover.q: Comfortable is a long adjective. What do we use with long adjectives?
discover.hint: Look at the words in front of comfortable.
discover.insight: Long adjectives: more … than / the most …

discover.ctx: the best place · the quietest room
discover.q: We use the best and the quietest to compare…
o: one thing with all the others in a group
discover.hint: The quietest room in… what?
discover.insight: Superlatives compare one thing with the whole group: the + -est / the most. Irregular: good → better → the best; bad → worse → the worst.

rule.title: Comparing things
points: Short adjectives: -er than / the -est (cheap → cheaper → the cheapest).
Two syllables ending in -y: -ier / the -iest (busy → busier → the busiest).
Long adjectives: more … than / the most … (expensive → more expensive → the most expensive).
Irregular: good → better → the best; bad → worse → the worst; far → further → the furthest.
ex: The café is cheaper than the library.
It is the quietest room in the building.
rule.watch: Never use more and -er together: more cheaper → cheaper.

practice.q: Living in the city is ___ (expensive) than living in the country.
Today is ___ day of the year so far.
practice.hint: Superlative. And look at the spelling.
practice.why: hot → hotter → the hottest: double the final t.

practice.s: This is the {goodest} restaurant near campus.

practice.q: My listening score was ___ than my reading score.

practice.a: Speaking is much harder than writing.
practice.hint: Start with Speaking… Much goes before the comparative.
practice.why: Use much before a comparative to make it stronger: much harder.

practice.q: Writing Task 2 is ___ (difficult) part of the exam for many students.
practice.hint: Compare one part with all the other parts.
practice.why: Superlative of a long adjective: the most difficult.

post.q: Brisbane is ___ than Hobart.
This is the ___ topic in the course.
post.why: Useful is a long adjective: the most useful.

post.q: Group work is ___ (easy) than presenting alone.
post.why: Easy ends in -y: y → i + -er = easier.

post.s: Speaking is {badder} than writing for me.
post.why: Bad is irregular: bad → worse → the worst.

post.q: That was the ___ lecture of the week.

produce.task: Compare two places where you can study (for example, the library and your home). Write 3–4 sentences. Use at least two comparatives and one superlative.
checklist: I used than after each comparative.
I didn’t use more and -er together.
I used the before my superlative.
produce.model: The library is quieter than my home, but my home is more comfortable. The library is also further from my house, so it takes longer to get there. For me, the best place to study is the library on a weekday morning, because it is the quietest time.

units.title: Much, many, a few, a little
units.cando: Talk about amounts with countable and uncountable nouns.

pre.q: How ___ homework do you have tonight?
There aren’t ___ students in the library today.
Can I give you ___ advice?

pre.s: I need more {informations} about the course.

pre.instr: Type the missing words: a few or a little?
pre.q: I only have ___ minutes before my class, so let’s be quick.

notice.title: A message to a classmate
notice.instr: Read the message. Tap every word or phrase that tells us how much or how many.
notice.text: Hi Sam, I don’t have [[much]] time this week, and I have [[a lot of]] readings to finish. There aren’t [[many]] books about our topic in the library, but I found [[a few]] useful articles online. Could you give me [[some]] advice? I also have [[a little]] money left, so let’s meet at the café. I’ll buy the coffee! Mia
notice.after: Look at the nouns after each word: time, readings, books, articles, advice, money. Can you count them? You’ll work it out next.

discover.ctx: much time · a little money · some advice
discover.q: Can we count time, money and advice (one money, two moneys…)?
discover.hint: Can you say ‘two advices’?
discover.insight: Uncountable nouns have no plural: time, money, advice, information, research, homework.

discover.ctx: not many books · a few articles
discover.q: Books and articles are countable (they have a plural -s). Which words go with plural countable nouns?
discover.hint: Look at the words in front of books and articles.
discover.insight: Countable plurals: many, a few. Uncountable: much, a little.

discover.ctx: a lot of readings · some advice
discover.q: Which words work with BOTH countable and uncountable nouns?
discover.hint: Readings is countable; advice is uncountable.
discover.insight: a lot of, some and any work with both. In positive sentences, a lot of sounds more natural than much: I have a lot of time.

rule.title: How much? How many?
points: Countable nouns (books, students, ideas): many, a few, How many…?
Uncountable nouns (time, money, advice, information, research, homework): much, a little, How much…?
Both: a lot of, some, any.
Much is used mostly in questions and negatives: I don’t have much time.
ex: There aren’t many books, but I found a few articles.
I don’t have much time, but I have a little money.

chips: We say ‘a study’ or ‘a piece of research’.

practice.q: How ___ people came to the lecture?
practice.hint: People is a plural countable noun.

practice.q: I don’t have ___ money this month, so I’m cooking at home.
practice.hint: Money is uncountable, and this is a negative sentence.

practice.s: My teacher gave me some useful {advices} on my essay.

practice.q: There are only ___ tickets left. Buy one quickly!

practice.a: We need a little more time.
practice.why: Time is uncountable → a little (more) time.

post.q: How ___ money do you spend on books?
There weren’t ___ people at the seminar.
Let me give you ___ information about the test.
post.why: Information is uncountable: some information (not an information).

post.s: We did a lot of {researches} for this project.

post.q: I have ___ questions about the homework. Can we talk after class?
post.why: Questions is countable plural: a few / some / a lot of questions.

produce.task: Write 3–4 sentences about your week: how much time, money or homework you have, and how many classes or assignments. Use at least four words from this unit (much, many, a few, a little, a lot of, some).
produce.target: quantifiers with countable and uncountable nouns (much, many, a few, a little, a lot of, some)
checklist: I used many / a few with plural nouns.
I used much / a little with uncountable nouns.
I didn’t add -s to advice, information, homework or research.
produce.model: This week I have a lot of homework and three assignments. I don’t have much free time, but I have a few hours on Saturday. I also have a little money left, so I might go to the cinema. My teacher gave me some useful advice about my essay.

units.title: Present perfect or past simple?
units.cando: Talk about experiences and finished past events correctly.

pre.q: I ___ to Japan three times in my life, and I want to go again.
She ___ her degree in 2022.
___ you ever ___ a presentation in English?
We ___ (not / finish) the project yet.

notice.title: A student profile
notice.instr: Read Lina’s profile. Tap every verb that talks about the past. Some are one word, some are two.
notice.text: My name is Lina. I [[moved]] to Sydney in 2023 to study nursing. In my first year, I [[lived]] with a host family, and they [[helped]] me a lot. Since then, I [[have made]] many friends and my English [[has improved]]. I [[have done]] two placements in aged care, but I [[haven’t worked]] in a hospital yet. Last month, I [[passed]] my first clinical exam.
notice.after: Some verbs are one word (moved) and some are have/has + another verb (have made). What’s the difference? You’ll work it out next.

discover.ctx: I moved to Sydney in 2023. · I passed my exam last month.
discover.q: These verbs are in the past simple. What do the underlined words tell us?
o: That the action is still happening
discover.hint: Is 2023 finished?
discover.insight: Past simple + finished time: in 2023, last month, yesterday, two years ago.

discover.ctx: Since then, I have made many friends. · I have done two placements.
discover.q: Do we know exactly WHEN Lina made friends or did her placements?
o: No, and it isn’t important: the experience or result now matters
discover.hint: Look for a date.
discover.insight: Present perfect (have/has + past participle): the time is not stated. The experience or result matters now.

discover.ctx: I haven’t worked in a hospital yet. · My English has improved since I arrived.
discover.q: Which time words go with the present perfect?
discover.hint: Which words connect the past to now?
discover.insight: Present perfect time words: ever, never, already, yet, just, since, for (up to now). Finished-time words take the past simple.

rule.title: Past simple or present perfect?
points: Past simple (moved, passed): a finished action at a finished time, often with yesterday, last month, in 2023, ago.
Present perfect (have made, has improved): experience or result up to now; no exact time; often with ever, never, already, yet, just, since, for.
Form: have/has + past participle (done, been, written, worked).
Questions: Have you ever…? Give details in the past simple: Yes, I went there in 2022.
ex: I have visited Melbourne twice. I went there last summer.
rule.watch: Don’t use the present perfect with a finished time: <s>I have finished it yesterday</s> → I finished it yesterday.

practice.q: I ___ my assignment yesterday.
___ you ___ the new library yet?
practice.why: Yet (up to now) → present perfect in British and Australian English.

practice.q: She ___ (live) in Perth since 2021.
practice.why: Since + up to now → present perfect: has lived.

practice.s: I {go} to Bali with my family last year.

practice.hint: Questions start with Have. Ever goes before the past participle.

practice.q: I ___ (just / finish) my essay. Can you read it?
practice.hint: Just = a very short time ago, with a result now.

practice.q: My English ___ a lot since I came here.

post.q: I ___ to Korea twice, and I’d love to go back.
post.why: Life experience, no finished time → present perfect.

post.q: He ___ his job last year.
post.why: Last year is finished → past simple.

post.q: Have you ever ___ a research paper?

post.s: We {know} each other since primary school.
post.why: Since + up to now → present perfect: have known.

post.q: They ___ (not / reply) to my email yet.

produce.task: Write 4–5 sentences about your studies or your life in a new place. Use the present perfect for experiences and results up to now (I have made…), and the past simple for finished times (In 2023, I moved…).
checklist: I used the past simple with finished times (last year, in 2023, ago).
I used have/has + past participle for experiences up to now.
My past participles are correct (done, been, written…).
produce.model: I moved to Brisbane in 2024 to start a master’s degree. At first, I found the accent difficult, but my listening has improved a lot since then. I have joined two student clubs and I have made friends from many countries. Last semester, I gave my first presentation in English. I haven’t visited Melbourne yet, but I plan to go in the holidays.

units.title: The passive voice
units.cando: Describe processes and research when the action matters more than the person.

pre.q: English ___ in many countries.
The survey ___ by 200 students last year.
Paper ___ (make) from wood.
Our essays ___ by two teachers.

notice.title: How the study was done (from a student report)
notice.instr: Read the report. Tap every verb made of is/are/was/were + another verb (two words each).
notice.text: This study looked at how students use their phones. First, a short questionnaire [[was designed]]. It [[was tested]] with ten students, and two questions [[were changed]]. Then the questionnaire [[was sent]] to 300 students by email. The answers [[were collected]] online, and the data [[is stored]] on a secure university computer. Every year, similar studies [[are carried out]] in many countries.
notice.after: Who designed, tested and sent the questionnaire? The text doesn’t say. Why not? You’ll work it out next.

discover.ctx: a questionnaire was designed · the answers were collected
discover.q: Who designed the questionnaire and collected the answers?
o: The researchers, but the text doesn’t say: it isn’t important
discover.hint: Is the person important here, or the action?
discover.insight: We use the passive when the action or result matters more than who did it, or when the doer is obvious or unknown.

discover.ctx: was designed · were changed · is stored · are carried out
discover.q: How do we form the passive?
discover.hint: is, are, was and were are all forms of one verb.
discover.insight: Passive = be + past participle. The tense is in be: is/are (present), was/were (past).

discover.ctx: The survey was completed by 200 students.
discover.q: What does by + person show?
o: Who did the action (only when it’s useful)
discover.hint: Who completed the survey?
discover.insight: Add by + doer only when it’s important or new information. Usually we leave it out.

rule.title: The passive voice
points: Form: be + past participle: is made, are used, was built, were collected.
Use it when the action or result matters more than who did it, or when the doer is unknown or obvious.
It’s very common in academic writing: methods, processes and results.
Add by … only if the doer is important: The study was funded by the government.
ex: Active: Researchers collected the answers. → Passive: The answers were collected.
Rice is grown in many parts of Asia.
rule.watch: Use the past participle, not the base form or past simple: <s>was build</s> → was built; <s>were wrote</s> → were written.

practice.q: Coffee ___ (grow) in Brazil and Vietnam.
practice.hint: Present simple passive: is/are + past participle.

practice.q: The bridge ___ in 1932.

practice.s: All the interviews {was} recorded and transcribed.

practice.a: The participants were asked three questions.

practice.q: Which sentence is more typical of a science report?
practice.hint: In a report, does the person or the action matter more?
practice.why: Method sections often use the passive because the action matters more (some fields also accept ‘we’).

practice.q: The essays ___ (mark) last week, and the results are now online.
practice.why: Past simple passive, plural: were marked.

chips: has grown is present perfect, active: no form of be.

post.q: These phones ___ in China.
post.why: Phones don’t make anything: passive, are made.

post.q: The interviews ___ in March.
Glass ___ (make) from sand.

post.s: The results were {wrote} in a short report.

post.q: Our class ___ by Dr Lee this semester.
post.why: The class doesn’t teach: passive, is taught.

produce.task: Describe a simple process you know (for example, how coffee is made, or how a survey was done). Write 4–5 sentences. Use at least three passive verbs.
produce.target: the passive voice (present and past simple)
checklist: I used be + past participle.
I chose is/are (present) or was/were (past) correctly.
I only used by … when the doer is important.
produce.model: First, the coffee beans are picked by hand. Then they are dried in the sun for about two weeks. After that, the beans are roasted at a high temperature. Finally, they are ground and packed. In our class experiment, the coffee was tasted by ten students, and their opinions were recorded.

units.title: Articles: a, an, the or no article
units.cando: Use articles correctly in academic writing.

pre.q: ___ study was carried out in 2023.
___ results of the study were surprising.
___ technology is changing how we learn.
He wants to study at ___ University of Melbourne.

notice.title: From a research summary
notice.instr: Tap every article: a, an and the.
notice.text: [[A]] recent study looked at sleep and memory. [[The]] researchers asked students to learn [[a]] list of words. [[The]] students who slept well remembered more. [[The]] study suggests that sleep helps learning. It is [[an]] important finding for students and teachers.
notice.after: When is it a, and when is it the? And notice: “sleep”, “memory”, “students” and “learning” have no article.

discover.ctx: A recent study looked at… · The study suggests…
discover.q: Why does the text say a study first, then the study?
o: A = first mention (new); the = the reader already knows which one
discover.hint: Which study? The one we just mentioned.
discover.insight: a/an = first mention, one of many. the = the reader knows which one (mentioned before, or only one).

discover.ctx: sleep and memory · students and teachers · learning
discover.q: Why is there no article here?
o: We mean these things in general
discover.hint: Do we mean particular students, or students in general?
discover.insight: No article for uncountable or plural nouns used in general: Sleep helps learning. Students need breaks.

discover.ctx: an important finding · a university
discover.q: Why an important but a university?
o: It depends on the first SOUND, not the letter
It depends on the first letter
discover.hint: Say them aloud: “a yoo-niversity”.
discover.insight: an before a vowel sound (an hour, an important); a before a consonant sound (a university, a European study).

rule.title: Articles
points: a/an: one of many, first mention: a study, an idea.
the: the reader knows which one: the study (mentioned before), the results of this study, the internet.
No article for general plural or uncountable nouns: Research shows… Students need sleep.
an before a vowel sound: an hour, an MBA; a before a consonant sound: a university.
ex: A survey asked 200 students about Ø stress. The survey found that Ø stress affects Ø sleep.
rule.watch: Don’t put the before general uncountable nouns: The technology is changing education → Technology is changing education.

practice.q: ___ research suggests that exercise improves mood.
practice.hint: Do we mean research in general?

practice.q: I read ___ interesting article yesterday. ___ article was about AI.
practice.why: First mention → an; second mention → the.

practice.s: {The} students need regular breaks to learn well.

practice.q: It took ___ hour to finish the test.
practice.why: Hour starts with a vowel sound → an.
practice.hint: Say it aloud: does it start with a vowel sound?

practice.q: ___ number of students has increased.
practice.why: The number of… is fixed; a number of = several.

post.q: ___ experiment was repeated three times.
post.why: We know which experiment (the one being discussed).

post.q: ___ climate change affects every country.
post.why: Climate change in general → no article.

post.q: She has ___ MBA from Sydney.
post.why: MBA starts with a vowel sound (em) → an.

post.s: This is {an} useful tool for students.
post.why: Useful starts with a consonant sound (yoo) → a.

post.q: ___ data from the survey was analysed in Excel.

produce.task: Describe a study, a survey or an experiment (real or imagined) in 3–4 sentences. Use a/an for the first mention, the for the second, and no article for general ideas.
produce.target: articles: a, an, the and no article
checklist: First mention: a/an; then the.
No article for general plural or uncountable nouns.
an before a vowel sound.
produce.model: A survey asked 300 students about part-time work. The survey found that students who work long hours have less time for study. Work can be useful, but sleep and study time also matter. The results are an important reminder for universities.

units.title: Relative clauses: who, which, that, whose
units.cando: Add information to nouns and combine ideas in one sentence.

pre.q: The lecturer ___ teaches statistics is very clear.
This is the article ___ I told you about.
Students ___ parents are teachers often read more.

pre.s: Canberra, {that} is the capital of Australia, is a planned city.

pre.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: My sister, who lives in Perth, is a nurse.
My sister who lives in Perth, is a nurse.

notice.title: From a report on sleep and study
notice.instr: Read the text. Tap each group of words that gives more information about a noun. Each one starts with who, which, that or whose.
notice.text: Students [[who sleep less than six hours]] often find it hard to concentrate. A recent study, [[which was carried out in 2024]], followed 500 first-year students. Participants [[whose sleep improved]] got higher marks. The researchers, [[who work at a university in Melbourne]], also found that phones [[that are used late at night]] can reduce sleep.
notice.after: Some of these groups have commas around them and some don’t. Why? You’ll work it out next.

discover.ctx: Students who sleep… · Participants whose sleep improved… · phones that are used… · a study, which was…
discover.q: Which word do we use for people?
discover.hint: Students and researchers are people.
discover.insight: who (or that) for people; which (or that) for things; whose = belonging to (whose sleep = their sleep).

discover.ctx: Students who sleep less than six hours often find it hard to concentrate.
discover.q: If we remove ‘who sleep less than six hours’, does the sentence mean the same?
o: No: it tells us WHICH students we mean
discover.hint: Do ALL students find it hard to concentrate?
discover.insight: This is a defining clause: it tells us which people or things we mean. No commas.

discover.ctx: A recent study, which was carried out in 2024, followed 500 students.
discover.q: What about ‘which was carried out in 2024’?
o: It’s extra information: the sentence works without it
It tells us which study we mean
discover.hint: Try reading the sentence without it.
discover.insight: This is a non-defining clause: extra information between commas. You can’t use that here.

rule.title: Relative clauses
points: who = people, which = things, whose = possession, that = people or things (defining clauses only).
Defining clauses say which one we mean: no commas. Students who sleep well get better marks.
Non-defining clauses add extra information: use commas, and never that. Canberra, which is the capital, is a planned city.
In defining clauses, you can leave out who/which/that when it is the object: the article (that) I read.
ex: The researchers, who work in Melbourne, found that phones that are used late at night reduce sleep.
rule.watch: <s>Canberra, that is the capital…</s> → Canberra, which is the capital…

practice.q: A person ___ studies the climate is called a climatologist.
This is the student ___ essay won the prize.
practice.hint: The essay belongs to the student.

practice.s: The University of Sydney, {that} was founded in 1850, is Australia’s oldest university.

practice.q: Choose the correct punctuation.
o: The book, that I borrowed, is overdue.
The book that I borrowed is overdue.
practice.hint: Can you use that with commas?
practice.why: ‘That’ is only used in defining clauses, with no commas.

practice.a: The app that I use for vocabulary is free.
practice.why: The relative clause goes straight after the noun it describes.

practice.q: Which word can you leave out? ‘The course that I chose is very practical.’
practice.hint: Who chose the course? ‘I’ is the subject of the clause.
practice.why: When that/which/who is the object of the clause (I chose the course), you can leave it out: The course I chose…

practice.q: My flatmate, ___ is from Brazil, is studying engineering.

post.q: The scientist ___ discovered penicillin was Alexander Fleming.
Is this the laptop ___ you bought last week?
I met a woman ___ son studies with me.

post.s: My laptop, {that} is five years old, still works well.

post.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: The students who passed the test can join the course.
The students, that passed the test, can join the course.
post.why: Defining clause: no commas. ‘That’ never goes between commas.

produce.task: Write 3–4 sentences about your city, your university or a person you admire. Use at least one defining clause (no commas) and one non-defining clause (with commas).
produce.target: defining and non-defining relative clauses (who, which, that, whose)
checklist: I used who for people and which for things.
My non-defining clause has commas and doesn’t use that.
My defining clause has no commas.
produce.model: Adelaide, which is the capital of South Australia, is a quiet and friendly city. Students who like the outdoors will enjoy the beaches and hills nearby. My favourite place is a small café that sells excellent coffee. The owner, whose family is from Italy, always remembers my name.

units.title: Although, despite, however, whereas
units.cando: Show contrast clearly and correctly in academic writing.

pre.q: ___ the weather was bad, the event went ahead.
___ the high cost, many students choose to live on campus.
Online courses are flexible. ___, they require self-discipline.

pre.s: {Despite} it was expensive, the course was worth it.

pre.q: City life is exciting, ___ country life is more relaxing.

notice.title: Paragraph: Is online learning effective?
notice.instr: Read the paragraph. Tap the words and phrases that show a contrast (a difference or a surprise).
notice.text: Online learning has grown quickly. [[Although]] it offers flexibility, many students feel isolated. [[Despite]] the convenience of recorded lectures, attendance at live sessions is often low. Some students study better at home, [[whereas]] others need the structure of a classroom. [[However]], a mix of online and face-to-face classes may offer the best of both. [[In spite of]] its problems, blended learning is likely to continue.
notice.after: Look at what comes straight after each word you found: a noun? a subject + verb? a comma? You’ll work out the pattern next.

discover.ctx: Although it offers flexibility, … · Despite the convenience of recorded lectures, …
discover.q: What comes after although, and what comes after despite?
o: although + subject + verb (it offers); despite + noun phrase (the convenience)
Both are followed by a noun
Both are followed by subject + verb
discover.hint: Is there a verb after despite?
discover.insight: although / even though / whereas + subject + verb. despite / in spite of + noun or -ing: despite the cost, despite being tired.

discover.ctx: … may offer the best of both. → However, a mix of…
discover.q: Where is however, and what punctuation is used?
o: At the start of a new sentence, followed by a comma
In the middle of a sentence, with no punctuation
discover.hint: Look at the full stop before it and the comma after it.
discover.insight: However links two sentences: Sentence. However, sentence. (Or after a semicolon: …; however, …)

discover.ctx: Some students study better at home, whereas others need a classroom.
discover.q: What does whereas do here?
o: Compares two different groups or facts
discover.hint: Some students… others…
discover.insight: whereas / while compare two contrasting facts in one sentence.

rule.title: Showing contrast
points: although / even though + subject + verb: Although it was late, we continued.
despite / in spite of + noun or -ing: Despite the delay… / Despite feeling tired…
however starts a new sentence (or follows a semicolon) and takes a comma: …. However, …
whereas / while compare two different facts: A is cheap, whereas B is expensive.
ex: Although the test was hard, most students passed. However, a few failed.
rule.watch: <s>Despite it was expensive</s> → Although it was expensive / Despite the cost. And never <s>despite of</s>.

practice.q: ___ feeling nervous, she gave an excellent presentation.
Some people prefer e-books, ___ others still like paper books.
practice.hint: Compare two groups in one sentence.
practice.why: whereas / while compare two groups (but also works; whereas is more formal).

practice.s: We went out {despite} it was raining.
practice.hint: Is there a subject + verb after it?

practice.a: Although the test was difficult, most students passed.

practice.q: The method is cheap. ___, it is not very accurate.
practice.why: However, at the start of a new sentence.

practice.q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Despite the rain, the match continued.
Despite it rained, the match continued.
Although the rain, the match continued.

post.q: ___ it was late, the library was still busy.
___ the noise, I managed to finish my essay.
post.why: Noun (the noise) → in spite of / despite.

post.q: Solar power is clean. ___, it depends on the weather.

post.s: {Despite} the course was short, I learned a lot.

post.q: My brother loves maths, ___ I prefer languages.

produce.task: Write 3–4 sentences about the advantages and disadvantages of studying abroad (or working from home). Use at least three different contrast linkers from this unit.
produce.target: contrast linkers: although, despite / in spite of, however, whereas
checklist: After although / whereas I have a subject + verb.
After despite / in spite of I have a noun or -ing form.
However starts a sentence and has a comma after it.
produce.model: Studying abroad can be expensive. However, it gives students valuable international experience. Although many students feel homesick at first, most adapt within a few months. Despite the challenge of a new language, they often improve quickly, whereas students who stay at home may have fewer chances to practise.

units.title: Distancing: It is believed that…
units.cando: Report ideas and claims with a careful, impersonal academic voice.

pre.q: ___ that the policy will reduce traffic.
The drug is thought ___ fewer side effects.
The building ___ to be over 500 years old.

pre.s: It is {believe} that the economy will grow.

pre.q: Coffee is known ___ improve concentration.

notice.title: From a report on coffee
notice.instr: Tap the phrases that report what people believe or say, without saying who.
notice.text: Coffee is one of the most popular drinks in the world. [[It is often said that]] coffee helps people concentrate. Moderate coffee drinking [[is thought to]] be safe for most adults. [[It has been suggested that]] coffee may protect against some diseases, but the evidence is limited. Too much caffeine [[is known to]] cause sleep problems.
notice.after: Who says or thinks these things? The writer doesn’t say. Why? You’ll work it out next.

discover.ctx: It is often said that coffee helps… · It has been suggested that coffee may…
discover.q: Why does the writer use these phrases?
o: To report a claim without naming who made it, and to sound careful
To give the writer’s strong personal opinion
discover.hint: Who said it? Do we know?
discover.insight: Distancing reports common beliefs or claims impersonally and shows the writer is not claiming them as fact.

discover.ctx: It is said that + clause · coffee is thought to + verb
discover.q: What are the two patterns?
o: It + passive + that + clause; Subject + passive + to + verb
discover.hint: Look at what follows each.
discover.insight: Pattern 1: It is said/believed/thought/known that + clause. Pattern 2: Subject + is said/believed/thought/known to + verb.

discover.ctx: is thought to be safe · is known to cause…
discover.q: Which is correct for a past action?
o: The site is believed to have been built in 1200.
The site is believed to be built in 1200.
discover.hint: The building happened in the past.
discover.insight: For an earlier action use to have + past participle: is believed to have been built.

rule.title: Distancing
points: It is said / believed / thought / known / expected / reported that + clause.
Subject + is said / believed / thought / known + to + verb: Coffee is thought to improve focus.
Past action: to have + past participle: The city is believed to have been founded in 1820.
Use it for common beliefs or claims you are reporting, not for your own findings.
ex: It is widely believed that sleep improves memory. Sleep is thought to help the brain store information.
rule.watch: Use the past participle: <s>It is believe that</s> → It is believed that. And not <s>is thought that it has</s> in pattern 2.

practice.q: Exercise ___ to reduce stress.
It ___ (report) that the bridge will close next year.
The painting is believed ___ by a student of Rembrandt.
practice.why: Past + passive → to have been painted.

practice.s: Social media is thought {that} affect sleep.

practice.a: It is widely believed that diet affects mood.
practice.why: It + is + widely + believed + that + clause.

practice.q: Which sentence uses distancing correctly?
o: Sugar is said to be addictive.
Sugar is said that it is addictive.
It is said sugar to be addictive.

post.q: ___ that prices will rise next year.
Green tea is believed ___ health benefits.
The castle is thought ___ in the 12th century.
post.why: Past + passive → to have been built.

post.s: It is {know} that smoking causes cancer.

post.q: The new policy is expected ___ reduce costs.

produce.task: Write 3–4 sentences about a common belief in your field or about a health topic. Use both distancing patterns at least once.
produce.target: distancing: It is believed that… / X is thought to…
checklist: Pattern 1: It is + past participle + that + clause.
Pattern 2: Subject + is + past participle + to + verb.
I used distancing for reported claims, not my own findings.
produce.model: It is widely believed that bilingual children learn faster. Bilingualism is thought to improve attention control. However, it has been suggested that the benefits may be smaller than once thought.

units.title: Participle clauses
units.cando: Write shorter, more academic sentences with -ing and -ed clauses.

pre.q: ___ the data, the researchers found a clear pattern.
___ in 1990, the theory is still widely used.
Students ___ in the online group scored higher.

pre.s: Having {finish} the experiment, the team wrote the report.

pre.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: Walking into the lab, the smell of chemicals was strong.
Walking into the lab, I noticed a strong smell of chemicals.

notice.title: From a research summary (invented example)
notice.instr: Read the summary. Tap the -ing and -ed words that begin a short clause. They replace longer phrases like who live or which was published.
notice.text: [[Using]] data from 2,000 households, the study examined energy use in Australian homes. Families [[living]] in newer houses used less electricity. [[Built]] after 2010, these homes had better insulation. [[Having compared]] the two groups, the authors concluded that building standards matter. The report, [[published]] in 2025, recommends stricter rules for new homes.
notice.after: Some clauses use -ing, some use a past participle, and one uses having. What’s the difference in meaning? You’ll work it out next.

discover.ctx: Families living in newer houses used less electricity. = Families who live in newer houses…
discover.q: What does the -ing participle replace here?
discover.hint: Look at the underlined words.
discover.insight: -ing participle = active meaning: families living… = families who live…

discover.ctx: The report, published in 2025, recommends… = The report, which was published in 2025, …
discover.q: What kind of meaning does the past participle have?
discover.hint: Did the report publish something, or was it published?
discover.insight: Past participle = passive meaning: published = which was published.

discover.ctx: Having compared the two groups, the authors concluded…
discover.q: Who compared the groups? Look at the subject of the main clause.
discover.hint: Who is doing the concluding?
discover.insight: The participle clause and the main clause must share the same subject. Having + past participle shows that one action happened first.

rule.title: Participle clauses
points: -ing clause = active: Students taking the course… (= who take).
Past participle clause = passive: Data collected in 2024… (= which was collected).
Having + past participle = this happened first: Having read the instructions, I started.
The participle clause and the main clause need the same subject, or the participle ‘dangles’.
ex: Funded by the government, the project ran for three years.
rule.watch: Dangling participle: <s>Looking at the results, a pattern appeared.</s> (The pattern didn’t look!) → Looking at the results, we noticed a pattern.

practice.q: The number of students ___ abroad has increased.
The questionnaire, ___ by 300 students, showed mixed results.
___ (read) the article twice, I finally understood the main argument.
practice.hint: This happened first: having + past participle.
practice.why: Having read = after I had read.

practice.s: Students {attended} the workshop received a certificate.
practice.why: Active meaning → -ing: students attending the workshop.

practice.q: Choose the sentence without a dangling participle.
o: Having finished the survey, the data was analysed.
Having finished the survey, we analysed the data.
practice.hint: Who finished the survey: the data?
practice.why: The subject of the main clause (we) must be the one who finished.

practice.a: Most people interviewed for the study were under 30.

practice.q: Reduce the clause: ‘The method which is described in Section 2 is simple.’
o: The method describing in Section 2 is simple.
The method described in Section 2 is simple.
The method has described in Section 2 is simple.

post.q: ___ a mixed-methods approach, the study combined surveys and interviews.
post.why: The study adopted an approach: active → Adopting.

post.q: ___ in plain English, the guide is easy to follow.
post.why: The guide was written: passive → Written.

post.q: Patients ___ the new drug recovered faster.

post.s: Having {wrote} the introduction, she moved on to the method.

post.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: Driving to work, the radio was on.
Driving to work, I listened to the radio.
post.why: The subject (I) must be the one driving.

produce.task: Write 3–4 sentences describing a study, a project or a process. Use at least one -ing clause, one past participle clause and, if you can, one ‘having + past participle’ clause.
produce.target: participle clauses (-ing, past participle, having + past participle)
checklist: My -ing clauses have an active meaning; my past participle clauses have a passive meaning.
Each participle clause has the same subject as the main clause.
I used commas after clauses at the start of a sentence.
produce.model: Using a short online survey, we asked 150 students about their sleep. Most students taking part were in their first year. Collected over two weeks, the data showed that students sleeping less than six hours felt more stressed. Having analysed the results, we recommend later morning classes.

units.title: Inversion for emphasis
units.cando: Add emphasis and a formal tone with Not only…, Rarely…, Only when…

pre.q: Not only ___ cheaper, but it is also faster.
Rarely ___ such a clear result.
Only when the data was checked ___ the error.
Little ___ (they / know) that the results would change everything.
Which sentence is correct?
o: Hardly had we started when the fire alarm rang.
Hardly we had started when the fire alarm rang.

notice.title: From an opinion essay on renewable energy
notice.instr: Read the paragraph. Tap the phrases at the start of a sentence where the word order is unusual (a verb comes before the subject).
notice.text: Solar energy has changed rapidly. [[Not only has]] the cost of panels fallen, but their efficiency has also improved. [[Rarely has]] a technology spread so quickly. [[Only recently have]] governments started to plan for a fully renewable grid. [[At no time in history have]] we had such cheap clean energy. [[Never before have]] so many households produced their own electricity.
notice.after: Each sentence starts with a negative or limiting word, and then the word order looks like a question. You’ll work out the rule next.

discover.ctx: Normal: The cost has fallen. → Not only has the cost fallen…
discover.q: What happens after Not only at the start of a sentence?
o: The auxiliary (has) comes before the subject, like in a question
The verb goes to the end
discover.hint: Compare it with the question: Has the cost fallen?
discover.insight: After a negative or limiting word at the start, use question word order: Not only has the cost fallen…

discover.ctx: Normal: A technology rarely spreads so quickly. → Rarely does a technology spread so quickly.
discover.q: There’s no auxiliary in ‘rarely spreads’. What do we add?
discover.hint: How do you make a question from ‘It spreads’?
discover.insight: No auxiliary? Add do / does / did, as in a question: Rarely does it…, Only then did we…

discover.ctx: Rarely · Never before · Only recently · At no time · Not only · Little · Seldom
discover.q: Why do writers use inversion?
o: To add emphasis and a formal tone
Because it’s required after every adverb
discover.hint: Is it needed for meaning?
discover.insight: Inversion is formal and emphatic. Use it sparingly: once in an essay can be powerful; five times sounds unnatural.

rule.title: Inversion
points: Negative or limiting word at the start + auxiliary + subject: Never have I seen…
No auxiliary? Add do/does/did: Rarely does it rain here.
Common starters: Not only… but also, Rarely, Seldom, Never (before), Only when / Only then / Only recently, At no time, Under no circumstances, Little, Hardly… when, No sooner… than.
With Only when / Only after, invert the main clause, not the first clause: Only when we checked the data did we notice the error.
ex: Not only does the app save time, but it also reduces stress.
rule.watch: Only invert when the negative word comes first: We have rarely seen this (normal) / Rarely have we seen this (inverted).

practice.q: Never ___ such a difficult exam.
practice.hint: Never at the start → question word order.

practice.q: Not only ___ (the app / save) time, but it also reduces stress.
practice.hint: Present simple, no auxiliary → does + subject + base verb.
practice.why: Not only does + subject + base verb.

practice.q: Only after the meeting ___ the problem.
practice.why: Only after… + did + subject + base verb.

practice.a: Seldom do students ask for feedback.

practice.instr: Careful: which one is NOT correct?
practice.q: Which sentence is NOT correct?
o: Rarely do we see such results.
practice.hint: Rarely at the start needs inversion.
practice.why: Rarely at the start → Rarely do we see…

practice.s: No sooner had we arrived {when} it started to rain.

practice.q: Under no circumstances ___ (students / should / use) their phones during the exam.
practice.why: Under no circumstances + should + subject + base verb.

post.q: Not only ___ the course useful, but it was also fun.
post.why: Not only + was + subject: Not only was the course useful…

post.q: Seldom ___ such a clear explanation.
Only when I read the feedback ___ my mistake.
post.why: Only when… → invert the main clause: did I understand.

post.q: Rarely ___ (it / snow) in Sydney.
Which sentence is correct?
o: No sooner had the lecture started than the power went off.
No sooner the lecture had started than the power went off.
post.why: No sooner + had + subject + past participle … than.

produce.task: Write a short paragraph (3–4 sentences) about a big change in technology, education or your city. Use inversion once or twice for emphasis (for example Not only…, Rarely…, Only recently…).
produce.target: inversion after negative and limiting adverbials
checklist: After my negative or limiting word, the auxiliary comes before the subject.
I added do/does/did when there was no auxiliary.
I used inversion only once or twice.
produce.model: Smartphones have transformed the way students learn. Not only can they access lectures at any time, but they can also join study groups from anywhere. Rarely has a single device changed education so quickly. However, only recently have universities started to teach students how to manage digital distractions.
